program: Cultural experience center / brand house / family learning and play space
one_sentence_summary: LEGO House translates the logic of LEGO bricks into stacked public volumes, playable roof terraces, and color-coded interior learning experiences.

key_facts.label: Project identity
key_facts.value: LEGO House / LEGO Brand House in Billund, Denmark, designed by BIG.

key_facts.label: Area
key_facts.value: BIG lists 11,960 m2; ArchDaily lists approximately 12,000 m2.

key_facts.label: Concept
key_facts.value: The architecture applies the ratio and combinatory logic of the LEGO brick to a public experience building.

key_facts.label: Public role
key_facts.value: The project combines paid experience functions with public urban interfaces, including plaza-like and roof-terrace spaces.

design_concept.sourced_concept: BIG states that the project applies the ratio of the LEGO brick throughout the architecture and embodies LEGO culture and values.
design_concept.ai_synthesis: The project turns the LEGO system into an architectural rule: stacked volumes, accessible roof surfaces, color-coded experiences, and a ground-level public interface.

key_strategies.strategy_name: Translate brand logic into spatial rules
key_strategies.design_problem: A brand building can become a superficial icon if the symbol remains only on the facade.
key_strategies.specific_approach: Use LEGO brick ratio, stacking, color, and combinatory logic to organize massing, facade order, roof terraces, and interior zones.
key_strategies.architectural_effect: The brand is experienced through space and movement rather than only through signage or imagery.
key_strategies.evidence: BIG describes the use of LEGO brick ratio; ArchDaily photos and drawings show stacked white volumes and color-coded roof and interior spaces.
key_strategies.transferable_lesson: When a project has a strong cultural or brand motif, translate it into proportion, organization, circulation, or tectonic rules.

key_strategies.strategy_name: Turn the roof into a playable public terrain
key_strategies.design_problem: Experience buildings often become inward-facing, ticketed destinations with weak urban publicness.
key_strategies.specific_approach: Stack volumes to create accessible roof terraces and outdoor play surfaces.
key_strategies.architectural_effect: The building becomes something to climb, inhabit, and use, not only something to enter and view.
key_strategies.evidence: ArchDaily photos and section drawings show roof terraces as part of the architectural experience.
key_strategies.transferable_lesson: Cultural and commercial public buildings can use roof, steps, terraces, and platforms as public interfaces.

key_strategies.strategy_name: Organize learning through color-coded experiential zones
key_strategies.design_problem: A family learning space needs active participation rather than passive exhibition viewing.
key_strategies.specific_approach: Arrange different experience areas through themed zones, color, and paths inside the stacked building.
key_strategies.architectural_effect: The visitor route becomes a sequence of making, playing, pausing, and discovering.
key_strategies.evidence: LEGO House official materials emphasize play and experience; ArchDaily interior photos and plans show activity-based spaces.
key_strategies.transferable_lesson: Educational and cultural projects should translate learning goals into spatial types, not only exhibition content.

key_strategies.strategy_name: Use section to connect interior experience and exterior public space
key_strategies.design_problem: Exterior form, interior exhibitions, and roof activities can become separate gestures.
key_strategies.specific_approach: Connect stacked volumes, floor heights, interior zones, and roof terraces through a continuous sectional organization.
key_strategies.architectural_effect: The building works as a continuous public terrain from ground to roof, rather than a closed exhibition box.
key_strategies.evidence: ArchDaily section drawing shows the relationship between stacked volumes, interior spaces, and roof platforms.
key_strategies.transferable_lesson: Use sections to test whether arrival, movement, interior activities, and roof use form one coherent experience.

spatial_ideas.text: The ground floor works as a public threshold where city access, arrival, gathering, and exhibition entry are combined.
The upper floors distribute experience areas through stacked volumes rather than a single neutral exhibition plate.
Roof terraces extend the play experience outside and make the building partly accessible as urban topography.

materials_structure.text: Public images and drawings confirm white block-like exterior volumes and colored roof and interior zones, but do not provide construction-level facade or roof detail.
The structural system, waterproofing build-up, facade assembly, and construction process were not confirmed in reliable public sources reviewed for this package.

site_context.text: The project is located in Billund, Denmark, the city associated with LEGO's origin and brand identity.
The project operates as a public-facing destination rather than only an internal brand exhibition.

location_role.text: Billund is central to LEGO's brand origin, making the project a destination tied to place and corporate culture.

natural_environment.text: No substantial natural-environment design constraint was confirmed in reviewed sources.

cultural_environment.text: The cultural context is dominated by LEGO's brand history and play-based learning identity.

terrain_conditions.text: Public sources reviewed here did not confirm special terrain constraints.

roads_and_access.text: The ground floor plan supports a public arrival and gathering reading, but detailed traffic organization is not confirmed.

surrounding_buildings.text: Reviewed sources do not provide enough surrounding-building evidence for a detailed urban fabric analysis.

served_users.text: The project serves families, children, tourists, LEGO fans, and public visitors seeking play-based experiences.

core_site_tension.text: The key tension is between a ticketed brand experience and a public-facing city destination.

diagnosis.text: The project reframes a brand house as an inhabitable LEGO logic rather than a symbolic shell.

positioning.text: The project sits between cultural building, brand destination, and learning-through-play environment.

strategy.text: Apply LEGO brick ratio, stacking, color, and combinatory logic across massing, circulation, and experience zones.

imagery_and_expression.text: White stacked volumes and colored terraces translate toy-scale identity into architectural scale.

function.text: The building combines experience zones, public arrival, roof play, retail, and visitor amenities.

layout.text: Ground and upper-floor plans show public entry organization and experience-zone distribution through stacked plan logic.

composition.text: Massing is composed as a stack of block-like volumes whose roof surfaces become usable terraces.

place_atmosphere.text: The atmosphere is playful and participatory, supported by color, scale shifts, roof play, and activity-based interiors.

construction_language.text: Public evidence supports analysis of the block-like exterior language and sectional stacking, but not structural-system specifics.

materials_and_craft.text: Public photos confirm white exterior expression and colored surfaces; detailed material build-ups are not confirmed.

tectonic_logic.text: The tectonic reading available from public material is primarily proportional and sectional, not node-level.

performance_and_construction_control.text: Roof terrace performance, waterproofing, envelope performance, and construction control measures were not confirmed in reliable public sources.

transferable_methods.text: Translate strong symbols into spatial systems: proportion, plan, section, route, and public interface.
Use roofs and terraces to make experience buildings more public and city-facing.

avoid_copying.text: Do not copy the colored block aesthetic without an equivalent cultural or programmatic reason.
